opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the motivation really came from looking at what our robot policies could and couldn't do. We'd gotten to the point where a model like π0 could do some pretty impressive low-level things, like folding laundry, bussing a table, or wiping a counter, when you gave it a fairly short, simple instruction. But in the real world people don't talk to robots that way. They say something like, "Can you make me a sandwich, but I'm vegetarian, and actually hold the tomatoes." Or they interrupt halfway through and say, "No, not that one, the other one." A single flat policy mapping an image and a short command straight to actions really struggles with that kind of open-ended, multi-step, sometimes-corrected instruction.

So the idea was to borrow a bit from how people think about it. There's a higher-level, deliberative process, a kind of "System 2," that reasons about the overall task, figures out the next step, and responds to feedback. Then there's a lower-level, more reactive "System 1" that executes those steps fluidly. In Hi Robot, the high-level part is a vision-language model. It takes in the scene and whatever the person has said and breaks that down into simpler, atomic language commands, things like "pick up the lettuce" or "put the cheese on the bread." Then the low-level vision-language-action policy turns those commands into actual motor actions.

The interactive part was really important to us too. We wanted the robot to handle feedback in the moment. If you say "that's not trash" while it's cleaning up, the high-level model can take that in, change its plan, and even talk back to you to acknowledge it or ask a clarifying question. That's something you can't really get if the language interface is just a one-shot prompt at the start of the episode.

One of the tricky parts was data. You don't have a lot of robot data where people give these complex, situated instructions and corrections. So a big piece of the work was generating synthetic data. We took the robot demonstrations we already had, segmented them into short skills, and then used large language models to produce plausible user prompts and interjections that fit those situations. That let us train the high-level model to handle much richer interactions than what appeared in the raw data.

More broadly, I think it reflects a bet that to get robots that are actually useful in homes and other unstructured settings, you need them to follow instructions you've never seen before and adapt as you go. The hierarchy gives you a clean way to bring in the reasoning and language understanding of these big pretrained models while still keeping control at the low level fast and dexterous.

r001.rationale: The response says a flat policy mapping images and commands directly to actions struggles with open-ended, multi-step instructions, then describes a deliberative process that reasons about the task and selects steps for a reactive policy to execute.

r002.rationale: It contrasts policies that handle short, simple instructions with contextual requests such as making a vegetarian sandwich and holding the tomatoes.

r003.rationale: It describes the robot taking in corrections during execution, changing its plan, and responding to the user.

r004.rationale: It states that the high-level vision-language model breaks the request into atomic language commands, which the low-level vision-language-action policy converts into motor actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the two things we care most about, generality and usability, kept pulling us in the same direction.

If you look at how people actually want to use a robot in a home or a workplace, they don't hand it a perfectly specified task and walk away. They say something vague like "clean up the kitchen," then they interrupt partway through: "no, not that cup, the one on the left," or "actually, leave the dishes, just wipe the counter." A single monolithic policy that maps pixels and a fixed prompt to motor commands is really bad at that. It can be beautifully skilled at the low-level motion and still be completely deaf to the person standing next to it.

So the hierarchy came out of a pretty practical observation. The high-level part of the problem looks a lot like language and reasoning: decomposing a long task into steps, keeping track of what's been done, incorporating a correction someone just gave you, deciding what to do next when something unexpected happens. That's exactly what large vision-language models are getting good at, and they get to benefit from all the web-scale pretraining. The low-level part looks very different. It's high-frequency, continuous control, and it needs to be reactive at tens of hertz with contact and dexterity. Those two things want different data, different timescales, and arguably different architectures. Forcing them into one network means the model is constantly trading off between them.

Once you split them, interaction almost falls out for free. The high-level policy is already operating in language, so a user's correction or a new instruction just becomes another input it can condition on mid-episode, instead of something you have to bake in at training time. And the low-level policy doesn't need to understand the full task. It just needs to be good at executing short, grounded subcommands like "pick up the sponge" or "open the drawer." That makes it much more reusable across tasks.

The other big motivation was data. Long-horizon demonstrations are expensive and hard to collect cleanly. But if your high-level model can be trained on a mix of robot data, synthetic subtask annotations, and plain human language, and your low-level model can be trained on lots of short skill segments that get reused everywhere, you end up with a much more scalable recipe than trying to get thousands of twenty-minute episodes of a robot tidying a house end to end.

I'll be honest that we went in a little skeptical. There's a long history of hierarchical robotics that got brittle at the interface between levels. What's changed is that the interface is now natural language, and the model on top is strong enough to produce sensible, grounded subtasks rather than a hand-designed symbolic plan. So the hierarchy stopped being a crutch and started being an actual advantage, especially for the interactive case where a person is in the loop.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a monolithic policy mapping pixels and a fixed prompt to motor commands with a hierarchy that decomposes long tasks into steps and decides what to do next.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes short, grounded action commands for the low-level policy from interpreting contextual user requests such as selecting the cup on the left or changing which parts of cleanup to do.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes incorporating a user's mid-task correction or new instruction during execution.

r004.rationale: It describes a language-based high-level policy producing grounded subcommands for a low-level policy to execute, with natural language serving as the interface between them.

astra-6.text:
The motivation is that there’s a gap between describing what you want a robot to do and actually getting it to do it. If you say, “Clean up the kitchen,” that’s a useful instruction, but it doesn’t specify every object the robot should pick up or every motion it should make.

A hierarchical system lets you separate those levels: reasoning about the task and what should happen next, and then executing the physical actions. And the interactive part matters because the robot won’t always understand your intent, and its first plan won’t always work. You want it to be able to ask a question or incorporate a correction along the way.

So the idea is to make the robot useful without requiring the person to spell out every step, while still giving them a way to guide it when it gets something wrong.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes task reasoning from physical execution, but does not say this works better for long-horizon tasks than a single image-to-motor-action policy.

r002.rationale: It notes that “Clean up the kitchen” leaves details unspecified, but does not identify a gap between policies trained on basic action commands and interpreting requests with contextual constraints.

r003.rationale: It says the robot should incorporate a correction along the way when its first plan does not work.

r004.rationale: It describes separating task reasoning and physical actions, but does not specify a language-specified next action as the interface between a prompt-reasoning model and a motor-control model.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was that we wanted robots to handle longer, more complex tasks while still letting people guide them along the way. A high-level instruction like “clean up the kitchen” involves a lot of decisions, and you probably don’t want to specify every individual movement. But you also want to be able to say, “Actually, leave that there,” or “Put this in a different place.”

A hierarchy gives you a way to separate those decisions: one level reasons about what to do next, and another handles how to execute it. The interactive piece lets the person correct the robot or clarify what they want as it goes. The idea is to combine autonomy with a useful amount of human control.

r001.rationale: The response says a hierarchy helps with longer, more complex tasks, but does not compare step-by-step reasoning with a single policy that maps images directly to motor actions.

r002.rationale: It discusses high-level instructions and user guidance, but does not identify a gap between basic action-command policies and requests with contextual constraints.

r003.rationale: It says people should be able to correct the robot or clarify their wishes while it is carrying out the task.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes deciding what to do from executing it, but does not describe a language-specified next action connecting a prompt-reasoning model to a motor-control model.
